facts: Accused individuals were prosecuted under Sections 272 and 273 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for food adulteration.
The accused argued that the special law, the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA), should apply instead of the general provisions of the IPC.
They based their argument on Section 89 of the FSSA, claiming it gives the Act an overriding effect over other laws.
law: Section 89 of the FSSA states: "The provisions of this Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force..."

The court cited a settled principle of statutory interpretation: if the main text of a legal section is clear and unambiguous, its title or marginal note cannot be used to restrict its meaning. The title can only be used as an aid for interpretation if the main text is ambiguous.
application: The Court examined the title of Section 89, which suggests its overriding effect is limited to "food-related laws."
However, the Court then analyzed the main text of Section 89 itself, which broadly states it overrides "any other law for the time being in force" without any such restriction.
The Court found the main text of the section to be clear and unambiguous.
Applying the principle of statutory interpretation, the Court held that the clear, unrestricted language of the main section must be given precedence over the more restrictive language in its title.
Therefore, the FSSA's overriding effect is not confined only to "food-related laws" but extends to any law that is inconsistent with it on matters covered by the FSSA.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument, holding that Section 89 of the FSSA gives the Act a clear overriding effect over any other inconsistent law, including the Indian Penal Code, concerning aspects of food safety covered by the FSSA.

law.description: Defines the offense of adulterating food or drink intended for sale, making it noxious. It requires the intention to sell the article or knowledge that it is likely to be sold.

Defines "unsafe food" as an article of food whose nature, substance, or quality is affected so as to render it injurious to health, and defines an "adulterant" as any material used to make food unsafe, sub-standard, or mis-branded.

application.description: The Court first examined Section 272 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), establishing that it criminalizes the adulteration of food or drink that makes the article "noxious" (harmful or poisonous).
The Court emphasized that a crucial ingredient for an offense under Section 272 IPC is the 'intention' to sell the adulterated food or 'knowledge' that it is likely to be sold.
The Court then connected the IPC's concept of "noxious" food with the Food Safety and Standards Act's (FSSA) concept of "unsafe food."
It reasoned that if an adulterant is added to a food article, and this addition renders the article injurious to health, it qualifies as "unsafe food" within the meaning of Section 3(zz) of the FSSA.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that if an adulterant is added to an article of food that renders it injurious to health, the food becomes "unsafe food" under the FSSA. The Court clarified that the concept of "unsafe food" (food injurious to health) is more comprehensive than simply "adulterated food," and further distinguished that sub-standard food is not necessarily unsafe food.

facts: The case involved the question of whether an individual could be prosecuted for the same act of food adulteration under both the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Food Safety and Standards Act (FSSA).
law: Section 89 of the FSSA gives the Act an overriding effect over other food-related laws.
Section 59 of the FSSA provides punishment for selling unsafe food.
Sections 272 and 273 of the IPC also penalize the adulteration of food or drink.

Section 26 of the General Clauses Act (GC Act) states that where an act is an offence under two or more enactments, the offender may be prosecuted under either, but shall not be punished twice for the same offence.
application: The State argued that simultaneous prosecution was permissible under Section 26 of the GC Act, which allows for prosecution under two different laws for the same act, as long as the person is not punished twice.
The Court rejected this argument by focusing on the specific language of the FSSA, which is a special law governing food safety.
The Court held that Section 89 of the FSSA explicitly gives its provisions an overriding effect.

Consequently, the Court determined that Section 59 of the FSSA, which specifically deals with punishment for unsafe food, will override the more general provisions found in Sections 272 and 273 of the IPC.
The Court distinguished a previous case that allowed simultaneous prosecutions by noting that the earlier case did not consider the overriding effect of the FSSA.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there can be no simultaneous prosecution under both the FSSA and the IPC for the same offence. By virtue of Section 89 of the FSSA, the provisions of the FSSA (specifically Section 59) will override the provisions of the IPC (Sections 272 and 273).

facts: The case involved interpreting Section 89 of the Food Safety and Standards Act (FSSA), 2006.

There was a conflict between the title of Section 89, which states it has an "Overriding effect... over all other food related laws," and the main text of the section, which states it overrides "any other law for the time being in force."
The issue was whether the overriding effect of the FSSA was limited only to other 'food-related laws' (as suggested by the title) or applied to 'any other law' (as stated in the main section).
law: The Supreme Court relied on a settled principle of statutory interpretation: the title or marginal note of a section can be used to understand the legislature's intent only if the main text of the section is ambiguous.
If the main section is clear and unambiguous, its plain meaning must be followed, and the title cannot be used to restrict or alter that meaning.
application: The Court examined the main text of Section 89, which states the FSSA's provisions shall have effect "notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force."
It found this language to be clear and unambiguous.

Because the main section was unambiguous, the Court ruled that it was not necessary or permissible to use the more restrictive language of the title ("food-related laws") to interpret the section's scope.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the main, unambiguous text of Section 89 prevails over its title. Therefore, the provisions of the FSSA have an overriding effect over any other law, not just food-related laws, whenever there is an inconsistency regarding aspects of food covered by the FSSA.

facts: The case involved the interpretation of Section 89 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA), which deals with the Act's overriding effect.
There was a discrepancy between the title of the section and the main text. The title suggested the FSSA overrides other 'food-related laws'.

However, the main body of the section stated that its provisions would have effect 'notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force', which is a much broader scope.
law: The Court cited the settled legal principle of statutory interpretation that if the main text of a section is clear and unambiguous, its meaning cannot be restricted or interpreted with the help of the section's title or marginal note.
The title or marginal note can only be used as an aid to understand the legislature's intention if the main text of the section is ambiguous.
application: The Court found that the main text of Section 89 was unambiguous.
The phrase 'any other law for the time being in force' clearly gives the FSSA's provisions an overriding effect over all other laws, not just those specifically related to food.
Because the main section was clear, the Court determined it was not permissible to use the narrower language of the title ('food-related laws') to limit the scope of the main text.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the clear and unambiguous language of the main section must be followed. Therefore, Section 89 gives the FSSA an overriding effect over the provisions of any other law (not just food-related laws) when dealing with aspects of food covered by the FSSA.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA) is a comprehensive and special statute intended to consolidate all laws relating to food. Based on its explicit statement of objects and reasons, which highlights the confusion and detriment caused by a multiplicity of food laws, the FSSA was enacted to create a single regulatory window. Consequently, the FSSA has an overriding effect on other laws, including general penal statutes, concerning offenses related to food. Therefore, prosecution for such offenses can only be conducted under the provisions of the FSSA.
legal_tests_applied: Purposive Interpretation of Statutes: The court analyzed the 'statement of objects and reasons' and the 'preamble' of the FSSA to determine the legislative intent, which was to consolidate food laws and create a single, comprehensive regulatory framework.

Special Law Prevails Over General Law: The court reasoned that the FSSA, being a special and later enactment specifically dealing with food safety, would override the provisions of a general law in the same field.

Interpretation of Sectional Title vs. Main Provision: The court observed that while the title of the overriding section might suggest a limitation to 'food-related laws', the main body of the section is not so restricted, granting the FSSA a broader overriding effect.
policy_considerations: The multiplicity of food laws creates confusion, which the FSSA was enacted to eliminate.
Multiple laws, standard-setting bodies, and enforcement agencies are detrimental to the growth of the nascent food processing industry.
The FSSA is intended to provide a 'single window' to guide and regulate all persons engaged in the food business, thereby consolidating the legal framework.
